text: A marriage ends, the wife has the papers to prove it, and the husband declines to accept the news. Morgan treats his own fantasy life as a residence rather than a hobby, and Karel Reisz films the upkeep of it as comedy: the energy it takes, the running argument with a woman who has moved on, the trouble with police who take his behaviour at face value. It was made in Britain in 1966 and shot in black and white, at a point when the Academy still gave monochrome costume design a category of its own, and this film took it. Grey rooms, grey streets, and a man insisting he is weightless. Ninety-seven minutes of farce played straight, in which everyone else's patience runs down at an ordinary human rate while Morgan's supply of invention does not.

The arrest is her husband's, but the bill arrives at her address, where there is suddenly no income and no plausible way to make one. James Ivory's film, made in France and in French, turns on the moment a married couple offers her a room, and on how long it takes an offer like that to show its terms. Hospitality here is a ledger. Three people share a household in which two already know the rules and the newcomer learns them at whatever pace they choose to teach her. A hundred and one minutes, kept close to interiors, with courtesy doing the work a raised voice would do in a coarser film. Nothing is demanded outright. It does not need to be. What is owed accumulates quietly, in rooms where everybody is being pleasant.

Two people, a table, and a man who has already decided how long the conversation is going to last. The threat is somewhere out in the city; the film stays in the room with the person who knows where. Stephen Reynolds gives the interrogator a partner from I.T., which quietly changes the shape of the thing: half the pressure is applied in speech, the other half in what a screen can confirm or contradict before the sentence being spoken has finished. Ninety-three minutes leaves no room for a subplot, and none is attempted, so every delay costs something specific and the costs are stated. What holds it together is an old bargain of the form. The one in custody is the only person present who is comfortable, and everyone else is on a clock he set.

A man flies to Australia to buy a car built in 1967 and ends up driving it into the desert beside a young woman who cannot see it. Clara Law keeps the Citroën at the centre of everything: a machine acquired as an object of desire, then put to the dull work of covering distance on roads with nothing on either side. The passenger gives the directions. The buyer, who can see perfectly well, follows them. Across a hundred and nineteen minutes the errand becomes something neither of them agreed to, and the comedy comes from how badly the etiquette of a purchase survives two strangers shut into a small French sedan. The Volpi Cup for Best Actress went to the performance in the passenger seat, which is where the route is actually decided.

A high school senior wants things, and a classmate has made a full-time occupation of getting them for her. Barbara Ann Greene's wants are not modest, and in George Axelrod's account of 1966 America they are not unusual either: clothes, status, a particular quality of attention, and the removal of whatever stands between her and any of it. Alan tells the story afterward, from a cell, so the terms are set before the first favour is granted. A hundred and five minutes billed as comedy that keeps sliding off the register, the laughs arriving a beat after something unpleasant, the school drawn as a machine for manufacturing appetite. What the film mocks it also films with appetite. That contradiction is why it still has teeth.

In Lyon, in a season when work is scarce, Marie is the rare person here who likes her job. She sells sex and does it with a hospitality Bertrand Blier films without irony and without apology: attention paid to the old, the heavy, the shy. Then a man sleeps in the entrance of her building, and she brings him a hot meal, then a place on the floor by the radiator, then herself. What follows is less a rescue than an economy. She has income, a flat, clothes to hand over; he arrives with nothing, and generosity on that scale does not stay level for long. The César for Best Actress went to the performance holding the whole arrangement steady. Ninety-nine minutes, and the tone cools by degrees without ever announcing that it has.

Almost nothing here is plot: a young woman with Tourette's syndrome, a man with no particular place to be, a car, and a border to the north. Bob Gosse has to decide early, and then again every few minutes, how to look at a body that will not keep its agreements in front of strangers, and his answer is to stay close and keep the car moving. Ninety-three minutes, one direction of travel. Road pictures usually promise escape; this one keeps depositing its couple at counters and motel desks and in other people's rooms, where the difficulty is rarely what the two of them feel and almost always what everyone else decides to do about it. Two people, a tank of gas, and whatever they can stand of each other.

A year after her husband was killed, a young man starts finding reasons to be near her, and he belongs, loosely and unhappily, to the organisation that killed him. Pat O'Connor puts that in the room and then declines to relieve it. Cal is on the fringe of things, which means errands, lifts, and a name known to people whose attention he cannot afford. Marcella is Catholic; her husband was a Protestant policeman. The romance offers no shelter from any of that. It is simply another place where the same arithmetic applies, and the film is honest enough to make its love scenes feel like exposure rather than relief. A hundred and two minutes, in which the tension comes less from anything anyone plans than from who is seen speaking to whom.

Cameras kept turning in occupied France, and that is the uncomfortable fact Bertrand Tavernier spends nearly three hours inside. Two men who make films go on making them: shooting days, permits, salaries, an industry that continues because industries continue, under an authority that decides who is allowed to work. The length is the argument. At a hundred and seventy-one minutes, compromise stops being a single scene of refusal and becomes a hundred small decisions about schedules and paperwork, each defensible on the morning it is taken. Nobody here is tested once and cleanly. Tavernier is interested in craft, in how a day's work is organised and what a production does with the hours it is given, and lets the occupation arrive through the logistics.

The table is set for a friendly game on Christmas night, and four of the five men sitting down have already agreed who is meant to lose. Pupi Avati keeps almost everything in one room and lets poker do what poker does on film: supply a clock, a currency, and a socially acceptable reason for men to stare at one another for hours. The mark is the only person at the table who believes he is among friends. The four who invited him have not been friends themselves for years, and what is left of that comes out sideways, in how a hand is dealt, in a debt mentioned in front of the wrong person. Avati took the David di Donatello for direction, and the proof is in how seldom he needs to leave the table to keep raising the pressure.

A magazine writer takes her daughter out of New York and down to the Louisiana bayou to meet relatives she knows only as names in a family story. Andrei Konchalovsky films the arrival as a change of jurisdiction: the visitors keep their manners and their deadlines, the household they enter keeps its own law, and neither side sees any reason to move. What accumulates over a hundred and eighteen minutes is less a clash of values than something physical, a matter of who owns the boat, who cooks, who decides when a guest may leave, and how fast a woman accustomed to conducting interviews becomes the subject of one. The water does much of this work. Distance out there is measured in engine time, and a house can be visited more easily than left.

A housewife from Bremen begins where anyone would begin: at a desk, with a form, explaining her son's situation to officials who are sympathetic and cannot help. The title supplies the rest of the address. Andreas Dresen plays a great deal of it as comedy, which is both the risk and the point, because Rabiye Kurnaz is funny, talkative, impossible to hurry, and the machinery she walks into has no procedure for a person like that. The film is patient about paperwork; it knows that most of a case is waiting rooms, forms, and long silences between answers. A hundred and nineteen minutes, and some of the sharpest scenes are ones in which nothing whatever is achieved. The European Film Award for Best Actress came out of the performance at the centre.

A woman dies unmarried and childless, and the fullest account of her life turns out to be in her own handwriting, in pages a young relative had no idea existed. What Taki wrote down is her employment: the years she spent as maid and nanny to the Hirai family, in a small Tokyo house with a red gabled roof. Yoji Yamada gives this a hundred and thirty-six minutes, most of them indoors, and the length is doing work, because a servant's knowledge arrives slowly, in overheard sentences and in the particular silence kept by someone paid to be present and not to notice. The reader is a young man in the present, holding a version of events he had no part in. Between his questions and her pages sits the real subject, which is what a memoir is permitted to leave out.

A rich man's mistress has been killed, and the household has already settled on the milkman. Suspicion here runs downhill, toward whoever delivers something to the door. Claude Chabrol treats that reflex as the actual case: whom a family finds it convenient to suspect says more about the family than any alibi will. The Marcoux house is the whole board, with a father who keeps an arrangement outside it, a daughter, and the daughter's fiancé, who is inside the family without being of it and is therefore the only one able to look at them straight. The investigation proceeds. The interest is in the rooms between questions, and in what a hundred and ten minutes of France in 1959 can show about people whose behaviour money organised long before anyone died.
